messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Using arguments (src/stan/gm/arguments/) as configuration; refactoring src/stan/common/command.hpp
parts:
I want to refactor the function:
    template <class Model>
    int command(int argc, const char* argv[])
 
It is currently 769 lines and RStan pretty much reimplements the whole thing to run most of the functions. (I haven't looked at Allen's code, but my guess is PyStan also reimplements all of it.)


One way to deal with this is to change the interface to something like:
    template <class Model, class SampleRecorder, class DiagnosticRecorder,
                     class MessageRecorder, class InterruptHandler, ...>
    int command(std::vector<argument*> arguments)

Each interface would be responsible for implementing the additional template parameters including the recorders and the "..." (tbd).
This function would then run based on what's passed in as arguments. It would be on the interfaces to translate to this argument structure.
This would allow interface designers to focus on implementing the different recorders, handlers, etc. and translate from the interface to an argument structure. This should stay backwards compatible always, so interface implementers can be behind Stan without penalty and being forced to change interface code with every new version.


Michael, was the original intent of the argument structure to be used as configuration?
As it currently stands
- there are no tests
- not sure how easy it is to validate configurations
- how would we handle changes to configuration over time?
- what helper methods are available for constructing a valid configuration?

For everyone else, anyone deal with configuration structures and have a pattern that they know about, is easy to maintain and implement, and will serve the purpose of capturing and communicating the configuration? Or... any thoughts on how to shape the arguments into something really easy to use cross-interface?

I think the stuff in src/stan/gm/arguments/ is almost there, but as it stands now, it needs a little bit more work to make it really usable. Maybe a combination of doc, tests, and factories might be enough? I'd love an extra set of eyes on the code.



Daniel

parts: Turns out I do have a lot of thoughts on this. More below.

On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:05 AM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> I want to refactor the function:

> template <class Model>
> int command(int argc, const char* argv[])
>
> It is currently 769 lines and RStan pretty much reimplements the whole thing to run most of the functions. (I haven't looked at Allen's code, but my guess is PyStan also reimplements all of it.)

That would be great. I thought that was where you
were heading when you dove into R in the first place.

This is also why I think the design for the current R
interface proposal from Andrew and Ben is so important.
We're thinking a 3.0 version that breaks backward compatibility
but is much more consistent along all these fronts.

> One way to deal with this is to change the interface to something like:
> template <class Model, class SampleRecorder, class DiagnosticRecorder,
> class MessageRecorder, class InterruptHandler, ...>
> int command(std::vector<argument*> arguments)

How about something like this:

template <class Model,
class SampleWriter,
class DiagnosticWriter,
class MessageWriter,
class InterruptHandler, ...>

int command(const CmdConfig& config,
const Model& model,
SampleWriter& sampleRecorder,
...);

The classes won't be enough unless they can all be constructued
based on the config. And this way the caller won't need to
specify the template args.

I very much like the idea of there being a config object
that the interfaces just populate. If the mapping can be
general, then that's even better.

The only reasonable pattern for something general and
nested for config is the following

Simple: properties objects map string keys to values,
where a value is either a string or another property
object

Sequence Values: Add sequence values

Numeric Values: Add numeric values.

With sequence and numeric values, we basically get something that
could be coded as strings in JSON and would have a direct analogue
as an R list or Python dictionary. Then we can share the doc, with
only the method of constructing the nested object changing. It's
not super idiomatic for R, but I like it --- we're breaking the regular
command-line idioms for the commnad-line config. I don't know about Python's
idioms.

Defaults and Inheritance: Java's Properties class implementation maintains
a pointer to a parent properties class (which may be null). Keys are
first looked up in the local implementation, but if the key doesn't exist,
the call is delegated to the parent class. The whole thing can be flattened
for transport.

I'm not sure the best way to nest this in C++. A general
approach would be to use the variant structures from Boost that
are used in the abstract syntax tree for the parser, which has
the same problem in that right-hand sides can be one of many
things and you want to act differently for each.

Consistency: if we can manage purely compositional consistency,
that would be awesome. doc, testing and maintenance problems arise
as soon as values or existence of one key can depend on another (e.g.,
model string or model file in current setup).

- Bob

parts: Thanks, Bob. I'll respond below. First, I wanted to get back to Michael's email.
On Tue, Jun 24, 2014 at 3:47 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

As it currently stands
- there are no tests
- not sure how easy it is to validate configurations
- how would we handle changes to configuration over time?
- what helper methods are available for constructing a valid configuration?
I think you missed https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/develop/src/test/integration/gm/arguments.

Yes, I completely forgot about those tests. But, they don't fix configuration.

I realized that these tests don't fix behavior and prevent others from changing behavior. I came to that conclusion from Marcus's lbfgs branch where he went through and added new argument items as well as changed existing configuration items. The addition of new items doesn't bother me, it's the change to the existing items that weren't caught that scares me a bit. If this is what interface writers are going to use as the interface into Stan, we need to make sure it doesn't change without forcing the developer changing it to be aware that it has effects beyond the class.

In particular, argument_parser_test builds up all possible combinations of valid/invalid arguments
dynamically and tests that each yields a valid/invalid configuration.  Valid/invalid values are
defined by each argument and the configurations are built up from the recursive dependencies
of each argument so that nothing has to be hand-coded.

As I was saying before, this sort of testing is more circular than I want it. Maybe it shouldn't be hand-coded, but perhaps we can serialize the current valid configurations to disk now and really force someone changing the spec to be conscious and think through the changes made to this spec.
The alternative is to have each interface define some intermediate object, say a configuration string matching what we input to argv in CmdStan and let the parser handle the unpacking.
I would not like to use a string as the configuration. I think that's really hard to maintain.

> Hi Daniel and Bob,

> That said, I'd urge erring on side of simplicity and C idioms for maximum
> compatibility with (future) wrapping libraries. For example, using a struct or
> an enum rather than a class when it's possible seems like a good idea.

A C++ struct is just a class where everything's public.
Is there a narrower notion of struct we can invoke somehow?
You mean something without methods? Or without virtual methods?

Enums are OK for finite sets of values, but most of our
config is nested in that you specify an enum-like decision
(e.g., HMC or NUTS, or sample vs. optimize), and then that determines
a further set of params.

So I'm not exactly sure what you mean by simple when we need
nested config, some of which takes values other than enums.

Is there something specific we need to avoid on the C++
side?

- Bob

> As I was saying before, this sort of testing is more circular than I want it. Maybe it shouldn't be hand-coded, but perhaps we can serialize the current valid configurations to disk now and really force someone changing the spec to be conscious and think through the changes made to this spec.

It seems to me that one of two things will happen.

1. It's easy to update the tests, so they won't test
that things stay fixed.

2. It's hard to update the tests, so the interfaces will
never get changed.

They will make people take a conscious step to change the interfaces,
but presumably they're doing that when they change the interfaces
anyway.

So we'd need to have something that tests current behavior, but
isn't just auto-generated.

To the extent we can make dependencies modular, we can test
those.

> The alternative is to have each interface define some intermediate object, say a configuration string matching what we input to argv in CmdStan and let the parser handle the unpacking.
>
> I would not like to use a string as the configuration. I think that's really hard to maintain.

Why? Seems like the easiest way to do things to me.
For instance, if we have something like JSON, that seems
more portable than passing objects around through Rcpp
or other interfaces. Not that I think it's the right thing
to do, just that it seems easiest.

- Bob

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Using arguments (src/stan/gm/arguments/) as configuration; refactoring src/stan/common/command.hpp
parts: On Tue, Jun 24, 2014 at 1:23 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

On Jun 24, 2014, at 6:28 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> As I was saying before, this sort of testing is more circular than I want it. Maybe it shouldn't be hand-coded, but perhaps we can serialize the current valid configurations to disk now and really force someone changing the spec to be conscious and think through the changes made to this spec.

It seems to me that one of two things will happen.

1.  It's easy to update the tests, so they won't test
that things stay fixed.

2.  It's hard to update the tests, so the interfaces will
never get changed.

They will make people take a conscious step to change the interfaces,
but presumably they're doing that when they change the interfaces
anyway.

So we'd need to have something that tests current behavior, but
isn't just auto-generated.

Yeah, I'm out of ideas. Not sure where we should be between 1 & 2.

I don't presume changes to the interface are conscious now.

To the extent we can make dependencies modular, we can test
those.

> The alternative is to have each interface define some intermediate object, say a configuration string matching what we input to argv in CmdStan and let the parser handle the unpacking.
>
> I would not like to use a string as the configuration. I think that's really hard to maintain.

Why?  Seems like the easiest way to do things to me.
For instance, if we have something like JSON, that seems
more portable than passing objects around through Rcpp
or other interfaces.  Not that I think it's the right thing
to do, just that it seems easiest.

Sorry, I really said the wrong thing. I would not like to use CmdStan's command line invocation as the string configuration. It feels a little too non-standard for me to be touting that as our public interface. But I'm happy to be out-voted here.
